tldr: The authors propose FWBC-VLA, a framework that estimates contact forces and base loading in real time solely from proprioceptive joint information without expensive force sensors, and simultaneously feeds them back into VLA action generation and Whole-Body Control (WBC) posture compensation. On a real robot, it demonstrates significantly higher success rates than existing methods in contact-rich mobile manipulation tasks involving large reaction forces, such as wiping a whiteboard and opening a door equipped with a door closer.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed FWBC-VLA framework. The sensorless contact estimator HSR-Force runs at 200 Hz to estimate external residual torques from joint information. It establishes two feedback loops: injecting force tokens into the 15 Hz VLA model, and supplying a force proxy input to the compensation generator that stabilizes the base.
overview:
Mobile manipulation using wheeled-legged quadrupeds combines high traversability with stability, making it promising for complex real-world tasks. However, in "contact-rich" tasks like pushing open a heavy door or wiping a whiteboard firmly, reaction forces applied at the end-effector propagate through the arm to the base, causing severe posture destabilization.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at generating actions from visual and linguistic cues, but they cannot directly interpret changes in physical forces resulting from contacts. Meanwhile, low-level Whole-Body Control (WBC) can stabilize the robot, but it cannot distinguish between task-relevant contact forces and external disturbances. Furthermore, retrofitting force/torque (F/T) sensors onto the end-effector introduces major integration hurdles regarding wiring, calibration, and cost.

To overcome this, the authors developed FWBC-VLA, which estimates contact forces purely from the robot's own joint torques and motion history without any external sensors, and routes this information to both VLA action generation and WBC whole-body compensation. A dual-LSTM estimator rapidly captures contact onset and sustained loading, delivering force tokens to the VLA and bounded base velocity compensation values to the WBC.

Evaluated on a real-robot teleoperation dataset of over 5,000 episodes, the method achieved success rates 30 to 40+ percentage points higher than existing VLA and force-adaptive baselines on tasks such as wiping a whiteboard and opening a door with a door closer requiring around 50 N of resistance force.
contributions: Proposed FWBC-VLA, a novel framework that estimates contact forces and base loading solely from the robot's internal proprioceptive state without external F/T sensors, sharing this information across VLA and WBC.
Developed HSR-Force, a dual-LSTM contact torque estimator that balances suppression of free-motion prediction noise with fast responsiveness to contact onset.

Realized a hierarchical feedback loop consisting of cross-attention force token injection within the VLA for end-effector action adaptation and a bounded compensation generator for WBC to suppress base destabilization.
Built and released the large-scale WL&Arm Dataset, comprising over 5,000 episodes of wheeled-legged contact-rich tasks collected via force-directed teleoperation.

sections.heading: Reaction forces destabilize the base: the wall faced by contact-rich mobile manipulation
sections.summary: Extending VLAs to mobile manipulation requires coordination between task actions and whole-body stabilization, as manipulation reaction forces perturb the base through the arm. Existing methods either rely on force sensors or stick to kinematics-only control that ignores forces. This paper proposes a sensorless framework that estimates forces and drives both VLA and WBC.
sections.details:
Large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly, expanding their scope from stationary tabletop manipulation to mobile manipulation. In particular, wheeled-legged quadrupeds equipped with an arm are compelling platforms: their low center of gravity and four-point support make them more stable than humanoids, while their wheels provide superior agility over traditional platforms across uneven terrain.

However, in tasks such as pushing open a door or scrubbing a surface, reaction forces exerted on the end-effector travel down the arm into the robot base, causing wheel slip and severe attitude disturbances. Conventional systems strictly decouple high-level action generation from low-level base stabilization, communicating only kinematic position commands. As a result, physical events like contact onset, sustained loading, and release are never fed back. The robot continues outputting its nominal trajectory while the base drifts away, leading to task failure.

While mounting a force/torque (F/T) sensor provides direct measurements, retrofitting one onto platforms not originally designed for it introduces significant issues: cabling complexity, added weight, reduced mechanical rigidity, and tedious calibration.

To resolve this, the authors conceived FWBC-VLA, a sensorless interface that estimates the contact state purely from the robot's proprioception (joint encoders, currents, and measured torques) and routes it to both VLA action generation and WBC base compensation.

captions.F1: Comparison of three paradigms in mobile manipulation. Conventional kinematic VLA (left) ignores forces. Arm-centric force-adaptive VLA (top right) overlooks base disturbances. The proposed FWBC-VLA (bottom) runs a dual feedback loop from a sensorless estimator into both VLA action adaptation and WBC base compensation.

sections.heading: The intersection of force-aware VLAs, sensorless force estimation, and whole-body control
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work across force-aware VLAs, model-based and learning-based sensorless contact estimation, and WBC for mobile manipulation. Most existing methods either restrict force feedback to the isolated arm or limit whole-body control to kinematic tracking, leaving a critical gap in handling base disturbances and manipulation actions simultaneously.
sections.details:
This work builds on three main research areas:

### Contact-Aware VLA Models
Recent attempts have incorporated force feedback into VLAs, but most focus strictly on high-precision arm manipulation, ignoring how end-effector forces perturb the robot's mobile base. Other approaches incorporate tactile sensors or multi-modal fusion, but force estimation from tactile signals is indirect, noisy, and difficult to interface directly with low-level Whole-Body Control (WBC).

### Sensorless External Force and Contact Estimation
Classical sensorless estimation techniques include Generalized Momentum Observers (GMO) based on robot dynamic models. However, they demand precise identification of dynamic parameters and suffer from actuator dead zones and torque ripples. Machine learning approaches have also been explored, but they are often limited to binary contact anomaly detection or struggle with sim-to-real transfer. Reliably estimating continuous contact forces during highly dynamic whole-body mobile manipulation has remained a major challenge.

### Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation Control (WBC)
Reinforcement learning and VLM-based whole-body controllers have increasingly tackled coordinated base-arm control. Nevertheless, these controllers rely predominantly on visual observations or kinematic models. When large contact reaction forces push the base backward, they lack mechanisms to differentiate between external disturbances and intentional task-induced forces. FWBC-VLA is designed to bridge this missing link.

sections.heading: Capturing force intent: a teleoperation dataset of over 5,000 real-robot episodes
sections.summary: Because no contact-rich wheeled-legged dataset existed, the authors developed a VR teleoperation system with force commands and collected WL&Arm, a large-scale dataset of over 5,000 episodes. The operator's pressing intent is recorded as a feedforward command alongside high-frequency joint data.
sections.details:
High-quality real-robot demonstrations are essential for learning contact-rich mobile manipulation. However, existing open datasets lack coverage of wheeled-legged robots executing force-intensive tasks. The authors designed a teleoperation system to address two key challenges.

### 3.1 Hybrid Teleoperation Capturing Force Intent
Standard teleoperation records only the operator's end-effector positions, leaving out the operator's "force intent"—how hard they intended to push against a surface. To capture this, the authors created a hybrid position-force teleoperation setup using a Pico VR headset and controllers. Trigger and grip inputs specify target forces along normal and tangential directions, sending them to the robot as contact feedforward commands. These force commands are preserved in the dataset as annotations; during training, they are kept strictly as metadata for evaluation rather than leaked as policy inputs.
Additionally, to eliminate the action space mismatch between pretrained VLA backbones and wheeled-legged robots, base outputs were parameterized as planar velocities and steering angles rather than per-joint commands.

### 3.2 Structure of the WL&Arm Dataset
The resulting WL&Arm Dataset comprises over 5,000 episodes. High-frequency joint states are logged at 200 Hz for the contact estimator, while 15 Hz demonstration actions are saved for the VLA policy. The task distribution consists of bottle pick-and-place (41%), whiteboard wiping (25%), and door opening (21%). For estimator calibration and evaluation, dynamic trials using calibrated force gauges with known weights of 0.36 kg (3.53 N) and 0.72 kg (7.06 N) are also included.

captions.F2: Breakdown of the WL&Arm Dataset (left) and control mapping of the force-directed teleoperation using Pico controllers (right). The left hand intuitively commands base motion and normal/tangential force targets, while the right hand controls arm end-effector pose and gripper actuation.

sections.heading: Dual-loop architecture: estimating forces without sensors to support VLA and base together
sections.summary: FWBC-VLA consists of the 200 Hz HSR-Force contact estimator, a 15 Hz VLA policy, and a compensation generator that stabilizes the base. Estimated external residual torques are injected into the VLA Action Expert as force tokens and transformed via the Jacobian into base velocity compensation commands.
sections.details:
The core design philosophy of FWBC-VLA is to use a single sensorless estimator to simultaneously allocate information to high-level action adaptation and low-level base stabilization.

### 4.1 Sensorless Contact Estimator (HSR-Force)
The measured arm joint torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{meas}}_{t}$ can be decomposed into the free-motion internal dynamic torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{free},t}$ and the external residual torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext},t}$. Instead of estimating fully calibrated absolute forces, this framework estimates the external residual torque in real time at 200 Hz.
The estimator is built from two compact LSTMs: a "History Expert" that takes motion and torque history to suppress prediction noise during unconstrained motion, and a "State Expert" that observes only instantaneous state to prevent prolonged sustained contacts from being absorbed into motion predictions. Their outputs are combined via a fixed gate $\alpha_t$, smoothly transitioning from history-dominant in free motion to state-dominant during contact.

### 4.2 Causal Physical Interaction Representation
From the 6-joint estimated residual torques, a contact strength scalar $s_t$ and its local temporal variation $\Delta s_t$ are computed to form a 2D interaction descriptor $\mathbf{d}^{\mathrm{int}}_{t} = [s_t, \Delta s_t]^\top$. This captures contact onset, sustained loading, and release.
Furthermore, damped least-squares pseudo-inverse Jacobian mapping projects joint residuals into the end-effector contact wrench ${}^{\mathcal{E}}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathcal{E},t}$ and the equivalent wrench at the base origin ${}^{\mathcal{B}}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathcal{B},t}$, generating directional compensation features.

### 4.3 Interaction-Conditioned VLA Action Generation
The framework adopts pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$ as the VLA backbone. Because the VLA runs at 15 Hz, a window of the most recent 60 ms of interaction descriptors (13 frames at 200 Hz) is passed through a GRU encoder to produce a force token $Z^{\mathrm{force}}_t$. This token is injected into the final hidden layer of the Gemma Action Expert via cross-attention. Conditioning on force at the very final stage avoids reprocessing the visual tokens, achieving lightweight computation while generating contact-adaptive action chunks.

### 4.4 Whole-Body Compensation Generation
To prevent the base from being pushed backward by manipulation reaction forces, an MLP-based compensation generator takes the base-frame force proxy $\hat{F}_{\mathrm{body},t}$, IMU attitude errors, and nominal base commands. The MLP outputs planar and yaw velocity corrections $(\Delta v_x, \Delta v_y, \Delta \omega_z)$, which are processed through deadbands, slew rate limits, and low-pass filters before being added to the WBC policy. This enables the base to brace firmly against high reaction forces without interrupting the manipulation task.

captions.F3: Overall pipeline of FWBC-VLA. Proprioception inputs on the left feed into HSR-Force to estimate external residual torques $\tau_{\mathrm{ext}}$. A 13-frame window of interaction descriptors is encoded via a GRU and injected into the VLA Action Expert via cross-attention. Concurrently, Jacobian-projected body-frame loads pass through the compensation generator to correct base velocities.

sections.heading: Real-robot validation: sensorless estimation accuracy and overwhelming gains from force compensation
sections.summary: The proposed method was deployed on a real wheeled-legged robot (M20S) to evaluate force estimation accuracy and success rates on whiteboard wiping and heavy door opening. HSR-Force outperformed existing estimators in AUC, and FWBC-VLA beat baseline methods by 30 to 40 percentage points during high-load contact stages.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a DeepRobotics M20S wheeled-legged quadruped equipped with a CM1 6-DoF robotic arm.

### 5.1 Standalone Force Estimator Evaluation (Q1, Q2)
HSR-Force was compared against learning-based baselines (NEXT, DF-MLP) and an identification-based Generalized Momentum Observer (GMO-SI). Evaluating unladen zero-force error (N-MAE) and contact detection Touch AUC (Area Under ROC Curve), HSR-Force achieved the lowest motion residual error and the highest Touch AUC. In dynamic validation with known payloads (0.36 kg and 0.72 kg), HSR-Force also yielded the lowest error.
Ablation studies confirmed that the History Expert reduces motion noise, the State Expert preserves sensitivity to contact onset, and their fixed-gate integration yields the best contact discrimination AUC.

### 5.2 Real-Robot Mobile Manipulation Evaluation (Q3)
Two real-robot tasks were evaluated: (1) opening a door with a door closer requiring ~50 N of push force, and (2) wiping a whiteboard with unseen marker patterns.
Baselines included modern VLA models (OpenVLA, StarVLA, $\pi_{0.5}$, Gr00t N1.6), force-adaptive methods using physical F/T sensors (ACP, ForceVLA), and FWBC-GT using ground-truth sensor measurements.
FWBC-VLA showed striking improvements. In whiteboard wiping, it achieved 76% in the wiping phase and 64% overall success, surpassing the strongest baselines (ACP and ForceVLA) by 32 to 40 percentage points. In door opening, it attained 56% in manipulation and 52% in full clearance, exceeding baselines by 28 to 40 percentage points. Furthermore, it performed on par with FWBC-GT which uses a real force sensor, confirming the practical effectiveness of sensorless estimation.

### 5.3 Ablation Study (Q4)
The authors isolated the force interface (FI) and base compensation (BC) components. Adding FI boosted the average success rate from 12.0% to 35.0%, enabling contact awareness and adaptation. Incorporating BC further pushed performance to 59.5%. Specifically during the door-pushing phase, adding BC produced a 52 percentage point surge, showing that base bracing is vital for sustained high-force interactions.

captions.F4: Time-series trajectories of contact estimation during door opening. From free motion (green) to handle contact (red), peak pushing (dark red), and sustained contact (purple), HSR-Force consistently captures joint residual torques and equivalent contact forces.
captions.F5: Comparison of whiteboard wiping with and without force feedback. Without force information (top), the robot visually executes wiping motions but lacks sufficient and consistent contact force, leaving ink uncleaned.
captions.F6: Representative real-robot rollouts. Conventional VLAs in the upper row (OpenPi 0.5, Gr00t) fail due to base drift or inadequate force. FWBC-VLA in the bottom row successfully traverses the door and completes whiteboard wiping.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: empowering robots to physically engage with the world
sections.summary: This work establishes FWBC-VLA, integrating VLA action generation with whole-body compensation using sensorless force estimation. By balancing manipulation intent with base stability, it dramatically boosts success in contact-rich tasks. Future directions include studying the precise impact of force errors and extending to other embodiments like humanoids.
sections.details:
This paper presented FWBC-VLA, which estimates contact forces from proprioception without extra sensors, coordinating high-level VLA task planning and low-level WBC base compensation. The causal physical interaction representations from HSR-Force adjust end-effector actions inside the VLA Action Expert while driving corrective forces at the base through the compensation generator. Real-robot experiments on demanding tasks—whiteboard wiping and heavy door opening—proved its superiority over kinematic VLAs and force-sensor-dependent baselines.

### Limitations and Future Work
While the utility of force estimation was demonstrated, a theoretical characterization of how estimation errors propagate into task failures remains incomplete. Looking forward, the authors plan to investigate broader contact sensing modalities and extend whole-body VLA control from wheeled-legged robots to more unstable, high-DoF embodiments such as humanoids.

takeaways: Even without external F/T sensors, a dual-LSTM architecture running on 200 Hz proprioception can accurately estimate contact forces and their temporal trends for real-world use.
Injecting force feedback into the VLA via cross-attention at the final hidden layer of the Action Expert (late fusion) is both computationally lightweight and highly effective.

In contact-rich mobile manipulation, adapting end-effector trajectories (VLA) alone is insufficient; projecting end-effector forces onto the base via the Jacobian to brace the chassis (WBC) is decisive for success.
For contact demonstration collection, hybrid teleoperation that logs the operator's pressing intent as a force command metadata label is extremely valuable.
limitations: The estimated forces are residual-based proxies rather than fully calibrated absolute Newton values, limiting generalizability across unseen friction regimes and substantially altered mass distributions.
Base compensation (BC) exclusively counteracts loads transmitted from the end-effector, ignoring external base disturbances such as direct collisions between the chassis and surrounding obstacles.
Evaluations were restricted to two domains (door opening and whiteboard wiping), leaving scalability across wider varieties of contact tasks to be verified.
